Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Avoid Medical Care: Seeking medical or psychological help, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Meera was forty-two when the fever spiked without warning, followed by a cramping so violent it doubled her over on her kitchen tiles. Within hours, she was on a gurney, the corridor smelling sharply of antiseptic and floor wax. In the emergency department, a tube was forced down her throat, and the world narrowed to the rhythmic hiss of the ventilator and the desperate, uncooperative flutter of her own lungs. She lay in the ICU for eleven days, waking to the steady beep of monitors and the cold drip of IV lines. When she was finally discharged, her body felt like a borrowed machine that had malfunctioned without warning. In the weeks that followed, Meera began noticing every shift in her equilibrium. A sudden stand from the sofa left her vision swimming, and she would grip the doorframe until the room stopped tilting. What frightened her most was how unpredictable her own physiology had become; she had come to believe she could no longer trust her body to keep her safe. She started scanning her pulse and breathing patterns before leaving the house, convinced she had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. When her cousin offered to drive her to follow-up appointments, Meera politely declined, telling herself she could not rely on other people to watch her back if her body failed mid-transit. Alongside the scanning, Meera noticed how quickly a heavy tool belt pulled on her shoulders, and how a few flights of stairs left her chest tightening. When a client’s basement drain backed up, she crawled into the narrow trench, the confined air pressing against her ribs. Halfway through clearing the pipe, a wave of dizziness washed over her. She froze, certain that breathlessness was returning, and dragged herself out onto the gravel, heart hammering. After that, she traded pipefittings for residential maintenance work, taking the elevator to upper floors and carrying supplies in a canvas backpack. She also learned to route around the new urgent care clinic on 4th Street, and when a friend’s apartment carried the sharp tang of bleach, she left without finishing her coffee. In the months that followed, these patterns settled into her days. She stopped answering her phone during evening hours, fearing a medical emergency call would force her into a hospital. When a neighbor complained about a dripping faucet, Meera told her she was too booked up to respond, though her schedule was mostly empty. She had long stopped scheduling routine blood work, and when a persistent cough kept her awake, she swallowed antacids instead of calling a doctor. Now, at forty-five, sitting in a community health center waiting room far from her old routes, Meera watched the clock tick toward her first intake appointment. She had come this far only because a persistent tremor in her hands had made it impossible to hold a wrench, forcing her to ask a supplier for a referral. What she hoped for was simply a way to steady herself; what she feared was walking into a room that smelled like the past, or waking up to find her body had betrayed her again.
